primitives.name: Proper Scoring Incentive
primitives.verbatim_quote: Research question Five strictly proper scoring rules share the same population-level incentive (report your true probability), but do they behave interchangeably as *training objectives*?

primitives.breakdown_regime: Interchangeability fails at finite sample and model capacity levels.

primitives.name: Beta Family Reward Shaping
primitives.verbatim_quote: - Five rewards: (1) S_log=y log p+(1-y)log(1-p); (2) S_Brier=-(p-y)2; (3) S_spherical=[yp+(1-y)(1-p)]/√(p2+(1-p)2); (4)/(5) beta family S_{α,β}(p,y)=-y∫_p1(1-q)w(q)dq -(1-y)∫_0^p q w(q)dq with w_{α,β}(q)=q^{α-1}(1-q)^{β-1}/B(α,β), evaluated at (2,8) (weights low-probability region) and (8,8) (weights near 0.5); Beta(1,1) recovers Brier up to a constant.
primitives.latex: \mathcal{S}_{\alpha,\beta}(p,y) = -y \int_p^1 (1-q) w(q) dq - (1-y) \int_0^p q w(q) dq, \quad w_{\alpha,\beta}(q) = \frac{q^{\alpha-1}(1-q)^{\beta-1}}{\mathrm{B}(\alpha,\beta)}

reasoning_traces.think:
The core insight is that while all strictly proper scoring rules align on long-run incentives for truthful reporting, their finite-sample behavior diverges due to curvature and gradient structure. Log loss penalizes confident miscalibration heavily, Brier balances squared error, spherical scoring normalizes probability space, and beta-weighted rules emphasize distinct probability regions. This divergence manifests in training dynamics—specifically, how gradients propagate through policy networks. The beta family allows tuning of these dynamics by adjusting shape parameters α and β, enabling emphasis on underdogs (α > β) or favorites (α < β). The BIN decomposition provides a diagnostic framework to assess whether gains from alternative objectives stem from improved information extraction rather than spurious calibration artifacts. Thus, the primitives form a coherent basis for optimizing LLM forecasting under structured uncertainty.
